newsitem.title: USA: U.S. commercial banks aim to broaden products.
newsitem.headline: U.S. commercial banks aim to broaden products.

text.p: The $540 million acquisition of investment bank Robertson Stephens & Co Group LLC by BankAmerica Corp is further evidence that U.S. commercial banks see a need to broaden their product offerings, analysts said.

More deals are expected but whether the pace will continue at the level seen in the first half of 1997 is anybody's guess. Some rumored candidates for acquisition would be expensive deals for all but the biggest banks.
Acquisitions of smaller "niche" or "botique" investment banks are more likely than big blockbuster-type deals, analysts said.

"They (the banks) want to expand their cross-selling to corporate clients and they want to do it with public markets securities products," said Peter Davis, partner at the consulting firm Booz-Allen & Hamilton Inc. "Buying existing operations with distinctive capabilities makes a lot of sense from a strategic perspective."
Monday's announcement that BankAmerica Corp will acquire Robertson Stephens & Co Group LLC for $540 million rekindled speculation about potential candidates to be acquired by other banks.

Donaldson Lurfkin & Jenrette Securities Corp rose 3-5/8 to 55-3/8. Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc was up 1/8 to 39-1/4. Hambrecht & Quist Inc eased 1-3/4 to 26 after rising sharply last week as rumors bubbled about a San Francisco investment bank about to be gobbled up.

Perrin Long, an independent analyst who tracks the securities industry, noted that BankAmerica was paying five times book value for Robertson Stephens. "Would Lehman or DLJ sell for five times bok value? No way," said Long. He said Lehman might sell for two times book value and DLJ might sell for 2.5 or three times book value.
Long said it was hard to make an exact comparison because Robertson Stephens is a private firm.
But Long said BankAmerica was making a "good acquisition," acquiring a firm well regarded for investment banking prowess in technology and high-technology health care.

Long and other analysts said a key ingredient in the BankAmerica-Robertson Stephens deal was an arrangement for $225 million of cash compensation for the firm's managing directors over a three-year period. That assures the people with the expertise and the "relationships" will stay around.

The issue of whether partners will stay aboard or take their money and leave is believed to be an issue that has slowed a sale of closely-held Oppenheimer & Co. The firm, specializing in brokerage services for high-net-worth individuals and institutions, has been on the market for about two years.
An Oppenheimer & Co spokesman was not available for comment Monday.
Last Friday, spokespersons for both Oppenheimer and CIBC Wood Gundy, a unit of Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, declined comment on a report in the Wall Street Journal that the two were talking.

On Monday, a spokeswoman for BankBoston Corp confirmed a report in American Banker which quoted chief efecutive Charles Gifford as saying the company had looked at Oppenheimer and decided it was not a good fit.
Elaborating, the BankBoston spokeswoman said the conclusion was drawn after a "very cursory, preliminary review."
One source at Oppenheimer said the partners there are simply holding out for a good price in view of all the activity that has been taking place.

Some banks have shown a propensity to "build, not buy" when it comes to getting into new areas. Citicorp, the second-largest U.S. bank, recently hired Putnam Investment Management Inc executive Peter Carman and gave him a mandate to build an investment management business.

J.P. Morgan & Co Inc's chief executive Douglas Warner III said after the annual meeting last month that in all the potential deals the company investigated up to that point, analysis showed it was better to build rather than buy.

Raphael Soifer, analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman, said while the circumstances are different for every potential acquirer, "as long as we have a strong stock market U.S. banks are much more likely to buy a small firm like this one (Robertson Stephenson) than to go for a large firm."
Bankers Trust New York Corp has a deal pending to buy Alex. Brown Inc in a deal worth about $1.7 billion.
Morgan Stanley & Co, the investment banking powerhouse, last week completed its merger with retail broker Dean Witter Discover in a deal that formed Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Discover & Co.

Davis noted that most of these deals are not based on earning back the the cost of the acquisition through cost savings. Rather, he said, "they have to get an earn back from incremental revenue and cross-selling" and that will be the challenge for the acquirers.
